raw_data.title: The dentate gyrus controls hippocampal representational drift
raw_data.abstract: Neural representations evolve across time and experience, a phenomenon termed representational drift. The function and circuit mechanisms of drift remain unknown, including whether it reflects intrinsic biological variability within the population or is actively controlled by circuit inputs. Progress has been limited because there is currently no known experimental means to manipulate drift without also altering an animal's sensory or behavioral experience. Here we show that drift can be experimentally controlled through targeted manipulation of upstream circuit inputs. We demonstrate this principle in the hippocampus by selectively manipulating dentate gyrus granule cells, which are thought to promote discrimination between similar experiences. Inhibiting granule cells during repeated experiences in familiar virtual environments markedly reduced drift in downstream CA1, revealing that representational drift is not simply an intrinsic property of neural populations, but is actively controlled by upstream circuitry. By experimentally manipulating this circuit-level control of drift, we further discovered that hippocampal drift is concentrated around episode transitions rather than accumulating continuously throughout an experience. These findings establish experimental control over hippocampal drift, revealing a structured, circuit-regulated process that differentiates repeated experiences into distinct episodic representations.

raw_data.title: CSF1R inhibition during cranial radiotherapy reshapes the immune environment and glial dynamics
raw_data.abstract: Background: Cranial radiotherapy (cRT) induces long-lasting alterations in the brain microenvironment, including changes in glial populations and loss of neurogenesis. Pharmacological depletion of microglia via colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) inhibition has been proposed as a strategy to modulate radiation-induced neuroinflammation, but its effects on other glial populations remains incompletely understood. Methods: Nine-week-old male C57BL/6JRj mice (n=60) received either a CSF1R-inhibitor supplemented diet (pexidartinib, PLX3397) or a control diet prior to and continued for 10 days after fractionated CT-guided cRT (3x10 Gy, 30 Gy). Brain tissue was assessed at multiple time-points up to six months post cRT using immunohistochemistry for markers of microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and proliferating cells. Microglial identity and repopulation dynamics were assessed using IBA1, F4/80 and the homeostatic microglial marker P2RY12, complemented by morphometric analysis. Results: Pexidartinib alone resulted in partial microglial depletion, whereas its combination with cRT led to near-complete loss of P2RY12+ homeostatic microglia at early time points. After discontinuation of the diet this was accompanied by increased IBA1+;F4/80high;P2RY12neg cell densities, consistent with replacement of the microglial niche by monocyte-derived cells. Over time, these cells exhibited gradual morphological adaptation but remained largely P2RY12neg, indicating incomplete restoration of a homeostatic microglial phenotype. Combined treatment accelerated astrocytic reactivity compared to cRT alone and did not prevent cRT-induced loss of neurogenesis or OPCs. At later time points, partial OPC recovery was observed in selected regions in the combined treatment group. Conclusion: CSF1R inhibition during cRT profoundly alters the composition and temporal dynamics of the brain its myeloid compartment, characterized by sustained loss of homeostatic microglia and replacement by monocyte-derived cells. Under these experimental conditions, microglial depletion did not mitigate key histopathological features associated with radiation-induced brain injury and was associated with accelerated astrocytic responses. These findings highlight the importance of timing, extent of depletion, and repopulation dynamics when considering microglia-targeting strategies in the context of cranial radiotherapy.

raw_data.title: Hidden Spirals Underlie Cortical Traveling Waves
raw_data.abstract: Neural traveling waves exhibit diverse spatial patterns, but the neural dynamics that generate them remain unknown. Here, we asked whether the apparent diversity of traveling waves reflects distinct dynamical processes or a common underlying organization obscured in recorded brain activity. We analyzed intracranial recordings from humans performing a working memory task and developed FOCUS (Frequency-flattened Oscillators in Cortex Unmask Spirals), a coupled phase oscillator framework that accounts for spatial heterogeneity in local frequencies to uncover latent dynamics underlying the observed waves. FOCUS revealed covert spiral dynamics underlying traveling waves whose recorded spatial patterns showed no overt spiral organization. These hidden spirals emerged only after accounting for heterogeneous local frequencies, exposing dynamical structure that was inaccessible from the recorded wave patterns alone. The centers of the hidden spirals shifted across the cortex between memory encoding and retrieval, linking their spatial organization to distinct memory states. Together, these findings reveal that apparently complex spatial patterns of traveling waves can conceal latent spiral attractors, uncovering a previously inaccessible layer of neural organization in human memory.

raw_data.title: A gene expression atlas of a juvenile nervous system
raw_data.abstract: Although the fundamental architecture of metazoan nervous systems is typically established in the embryo, substantial numbers of neurons are added during post-natal development while existing neurons expand in size, refine connectivity, and undergo additional differentiation. To reveal the underlying molecular determinants of postembryonic neurogenesis and maturation, we have produced gene expression profiles of all neuron types and their progenitors in the first larval stage (L1) of C. elegans. Comparisons of the L1 profile to the embryo and to the later L4 larval stage identified thousands of differentially expressed genes across individual neurons throughout the nervous system. Key neuropeptide signaling networks, for example, are remodeled during larval development. Gene regulatory network analysis revealed potential transcription factors driving the temporal changes in gene expression across the nervous system, including a broad role for the heterochronic transcription factor lin-14. We utilized available connectomic data of juvenile animals in combination with our neuron-specific atlas to identify potential molecular determinants of membrane contact and synaptic connectivity. These expression data are available through a user-friendly interface at CeNGEN.org for independent investigations of the maturation, connectivity and function of a developing nervous system.

raw_data.title: Environmental dynamics shape human learning: change points versus random walks
raw_data.abstract: Adaptive learning requires interpreting prediction errors in light of environmental dynamics. However, environments may differ not only in when changes occur, but also in how they occur: some nonstationary processes drift gradually, whereas others change abruptly. This raises the question of whether humans can adapt their learning to the generative structure of their environment. Here, we compared learning in two canonical nonstationary environments: abrupt change points versus gradual random walks. Across two behavioral experiments using a predictive inference task and a unified Bayesian framework, we show that participants adjust their learning to the dynamics of their environment. Cross-validated model comparison showed that the environment-matched model best explained behavior in nearly all participants. Human apparent learning rates also showed the predicted dynamics-specific signature, increasing more sharply with prediction-error magnitude under change points compared to random walks. Participants tracked the changing latent variance (environmental stochasticity) online in both environments, jointly with the latent mean, through coordinated adjustments of paddle width and location. In the change-point environment, their width adjustments further distinguished changes in variance from changes in mean. Together, these results show that humans adapt their learning to both how latent states change and which properties are changing. They establish a unified computational account of adaptive learning across different environmental dynamics.

raw_data.title: What drives intersubject correlation of EEG during auditory narratives?
raw_data.abstract: When participants are engaged with auditory narratives, physiological and neural signals exhibit temporal correlations between subjects. The intersubject correlation (ISC) increases when attention is directed to the stories, suggesting that shared neural and bodily dynamics arise from a similar processing of the narratives. In this study, we investigated whether the ISC of the EEG elicited by auditory narratives is driven by low-level acoustic (envelope, spectrogram) and/or higher-level linguistic information (word onset, word surprisal) in two groups of healthy participants during passive, attentive and distracted listening. We use temporal response functions (TRFs) for acoustic, and linguistic features to assess the contribution of each feature to the ISC, measured using correlated component analysis (CorrCA). TRFs derived for acoustic features explained a larger fraction of variance in the EEG than linguistic features and were the main contributors to the ISC. The attention-related increase in ISC was driven by all features. Importantly, word surprisal had an effect on ISC only during active story engagement, with timing and scalp distribution consistent with language processing. Notably, the linear responses captured by TRFs only explained a small amount of the overall ISC, suggesting that ISC is largely driven by nonlinear responses to the narratives. Identifying the factors that drive these common neural responses, is clinically relevant for interpreting EEG ISC exhibited in unresponsive patients. We propose that the combined use of ISC and TRFs has the potential to provide meaningful markers of language processing in patients with disorders of consciousness, and we suggest practical recommendations for implementing these approaches in clinical settings.

raw_data.title: Individual variation in the accuracy of saccades to sounds is correlated with the properties of eye movement-related eardrum oscillations (EMREOs)
raw_data.abstract: Calibration of sound localization behavior in species with mobile eyes requires not only accurate visual input but also accurate oculomotor signals across the lifespan. The recent discovery of eye movement-related eardrum oscillations suggest that oculomotor signals may be incorporated into auditory processing at the level of the ear. One inference of this discovery is that individual variation in such signals might be correlated with individual variation in sound localization accuracy. Here, we tested this hypothesis in humans with normal hearing. We discovered that there is considerable variation in the accuracy of saccades to sounds even in normal individuals: median horizontal errors ranged from 2-6 deg., and median vertical errors could be as large as 36 deg. We separated the subject pool into groups with 'good' performance (median vectorial error < 8 deg) vs 'poor' performance (median vectorial error > 10 deg) and evaluated their respective EMREOs. The EMREOs differed across the two groups in how horizontal saccade amplitude and vertical initial eye position were encoded, with considerable individual variation in the 'poor' group. These results are consistent with the interpretation that EMREOs are associated with underlying processes that ensure the accuracy of sound localization.

raw_data.title: Motor automaticity in natural keyboard typing
raw_data.abstract: Certain features of everyday motor skills become automatic while others remain controlled. Here we use a novel keyboard typing task to investigate whether motor automaticity depends on the frequency of naturally learned motor sequences. Participants type five-letter strings that vary in their word and bigram (two-letter sequence) frequency in natural language, allowing us to examine the influence of prior exposure without laboratory training. Novel pseudo word strings are tested as well. We find greater sequence frequency in natural language is associated with faster inter-keypress intervals and lower temporal variability within the sequence. In contrast, latencies to initiate a sequence are slower for novel pseudo-word strings but are otherwise insensitive to natural word frequency. We also find individual differences in inter-keypress speed and variability are robust across frequency levels but are unrelated to conventional measures of typing skill. Our method establishes keyboard typing as a scalable, ethologically valid framework for probing features of a naturally acquired human motor skill. This research will help extend laboratory-based studies of motor sequence learning and sets the stage for future investigations of linguo-motor processes. Moreover, our findings demonstrate which features within naturally acquired motor sequences become automatic and that typing proficiency is not determined solely by automaticity.

raw_data.title: Evidence-Gated Plasticity and Context-Dependent Consolidation for Multi-Goal Learning in Spiking Neural Networks
raw_data.abstract: Background / Introduction: Biologically inspired spiking neural networks offer a mechanistic framework for adaptive behavior, yet learning multiple goals remains challenging when synaptic updates for different targets interfere. We investigated whether multi-timescale plasticity and context-specific credit assignment improve interleaved multi-goal learning in a spiking navigation system inspired by entorhinal-hippocampal circuitry. Methods: We introduce evidence-gated plasticity (EGP), in which reward-modulated spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) generates transient synaptic proposals and need-weighted behavioral evidence modulates their slower consolidation into durable weights. Global EGP pools these proposals and the corresponding evidence across goals. Target-context EGP extends this framework through goal-specific proposal and evidence stores and additional need-dependent scaling of consolidation. We compared the algorithms across paired spiking networks, tested learned weights with plasticity disabled, and examined upstream representations and consolidation components. Results: Global EGP supported multi-goal learning and durable navigation. Target-context EGP improved early reward across 40 paired networks, including an independently specified 30-pair replication. Across eight paired networks trained for 2000 episodes, target-context EGP maintained a reward advantage, increased target-contact success, and reduced expected time to reach the target when unsuccessful blocks were included. Independent fixed-weight evaluation demonstrated durable navigation in both algorithms, with seven of eight networks favoring target-context EGP. A component experiment reproduced the target-context reward advantage and identified additional need-dependent scaling of context-specific consolidation as the only component with adjusted statistical support for improved reward. Conclusions: EGP supports durable multi-goal learning in spiking neural networks, and its target-context extension improves acquisition and conditional target selectivity in this interleaved navigation task. The framework offers a basis for testing context-sensitive, evidence-modulated plasticity in other multi-context learning problems.

raw_data.title: Upregulation of Calbindin in Adult Inhibitory Neurons Reactivates Critical Period Plasticity in Mouse Visual Cortex
raw_data.abstract: Critical periods are windows of peak learning performance where heightened synaptic plasticity enables fast, robust reorganization in juvenile brain circuits. Unlike adult plasticity which requires ongoing, persistent change in sensory experience, cortical representations can be rapidly changed during critical periods and have enduring effects. Transplantation of GABAergic inhibitory neurons has been shown to restore critical period plasticity to recipient circuits by triggering signalling changes within host inhibitory neurons. Here we transcriptionally profiled host inhibitory neurons in mouse primary visual cortex (V1) to detect gene expression changes during transplant-induced plasticity. Gene ontology enrichment analysis of differentially-expressed (DE) transcripts in host inhibitory neurons revealed synaptic plasticity- and inhibitory neuron development-related profiles. We assessed the protein expression of a top DE candidate, the calcium-binding protein Calbindin (Calb1), across transplant conditions and developmental stages. We found high Calb1 expression during the V1 critical period and during transplant-induced plasticity. To assess the functional significance of transplant-reactivated DE gene activity on visual cortical plasticity, we developed a set of AAVs to manipulate Calb1 expression specifically within inhibitory neurons. Using intrinsic signal imaging to measure ocular dominance plasticity, we found that Calb1 levels in V1 inhibitory neurons determine the extent of visual cortical plasticity. Our study provides evidence that direct induction of critical period-stage gene expression patterns in inhibitory neurons restores juvenile plasticity in targeted adult cortical circuits.

raw_data.title: Dementia Language Models: a generalizable and controllable representation of cognitive impairment
raw_data.abstract: We introduce Dementia Language Models (DeLMs)--generalizable and controllable representations of cognitive impairment through language--alongside an evaluation framework for establishing their validity and clinical grounding. DeLMs created by fine-tuning large language models on a small clinical corpus successfully generated patient-like narratives across unseen tasks, received predicted Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores in the impaired range, and produced narratives that neurologists identified with accuracy comparable to real transcripts. The models' internal representations, as well as their non-linguistic decision-making, supported mild cognitive impairment detection in unseen cohorts. The effect was controllable: moving from Healthy toward Dementia in weight space progressively worsened language and predicted MMSE scores while increasing dementia probability. DeLMs could support clinician training, hypothesis generation, and scalable experimentation, reserving patient involvement for where it is truly needed.

raw_data.title: Hunger reconfigures a reward learning circuit into a memory competent mode
raw_data.abstract: Internal states such as hunger dynamically reshape activity across circuits to support resource seeking. Neuromodulation provides a means of controlling such physiological properties of neurons, but how this flexibility regulates memory networks remains unclear. Here, we describe how hunger reconfigures a dopaminergic food-reward circuit between two physiological modes that support memory formation, in Drosophila. Starvation suppresses baseline dopaminergic activity through peptidergic signalling, enabling reward-evoked, large-amplitude dopamine neuron spikes to reinforce learning. This spiking mode can be engaged by sugar consumption and persists beyond feeding, reflecting the fly's satiety state. Persistent dopaminergic large-amplitude spiking reinforces learning and transitions the memory network into a mode that prioritizes consolidation of recently acquired memories. The transition from hunger to satiation is also reflected in the activity of postsynaptic output neurons that shift from a tonic, decorrelated mode that is responsive to dopamine into a bursting, correlated mode in which further dopaminergic modulation is occluded. Therefore, nutrient deprivation reconfigures the memory circuit into a learning competent dopamine-receptive mode, which persistent reinforcing dopamine then switches into a satiated mode driving memory consolidation. Together these processes mechanistically intertwine state-dependent reward-signalling with subsequent memory stabilization through transitions in physiological mode.

raw_data.title: Multimodal Glymphatic Imaging in Multiple Sclerosis: Associations with Sleep and Disability
raw_data.abstract: The glymphatic system is the waste clearance pathway in the central nervous system. Although its dysfunction has been associated with several neurological disorders, its role in multiple sclerosis (MS) remains poorly understood. This system is thought to be particularly active during sleep, yet the relationship between sleep metrics and MRI-derived markers of glymphatic activity has been scarcely explored. In this study, we aimed to perform a multimodal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment of glymphatic function in MS and investigate its association with sleep parameters, clinical disability, disease duration and MRI-derived structural markers. The study included 22 patients (34.3{+/-}10.1 years; 16 female) with relapsing-remitting MS and 26 healthy controls (32.2{+/-}5.7 years; 18 female), all of whom underwent 3.0 Tesla MRI. Glymphatic function was assessed using diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index and global blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) coupling. In addition, sleep micro- and macrostructural features, clinical disability, disease duration, along with mean diffusivity (MD), lateral ventricular, choroid plexus volumes and lesion load were evaluated. Patients showed reduced DTI-ALPS index, though this difference became only a trend after controlling for MD. No significant group differences were observed in global BOLD signal-CSF coupling. However, in patients, the weaker coupling was associated with longer total sleep time, lower arousal index, greater disability and lateral ventricle enlargement, whereas the DTI-ALPS index showed no significant correlations with any of the measures. Together, these findings challenge the assumption that DTI-ALPS can serve as a reliable marker of glymphatic function in demyelinating diseases such as MS, where disease-related alterations in white matter microstructure can confound diffusion-based measures. In contrast, gBOLD-CSF coupling showed associations with sleep, clinical disability and structural changes in patients, despite the absence of a significant group-level difference. This finding suggests that gBOLD-CSF coupling may capture individual variability in glymphatic-related dynamics relevant to sleep and the clinical expression of MS.

raw_data.title: Identifying Network Factors Driving Changes in Brain Connectivity During Aging via Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models
authors: for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
raw_data.abstract: Brain network organization emerges from ongoing network dynamics that continuously create, maintain, and reorganize connectivity patterns. At both the structural and functional levels, these dynamics shape network evolution throughout the lifespan. Here, we introduce a data-driven framework based on Stochastic Actor-Oriented Models (SAOMs), which model longitudinal network changes as a process of local edge formation and dissolution driven by local-connectivity factors. Applied to functional and structural brain networks from an aging cohort, the resulting models recovered a set of interacting mechanisms that collectively promote hub formation, short-range connectivity, and modular organization. These factors were derived through a novel data-driven factor-selection procedure rather than specified a priori, allowing network mechanisms underlying longitudinal change to be identified directly from observations. Functional networks exhibited substantially higher rates of change than structural networks, suggesting more frequent opportunities for network maintenance and reorganization. Structural networks additionally showed despecification in the hub-forming mechanisms with cognitive impairment. These results support a view of brain network organization as an actively maintained process emerging from ongoing local connectivity dynamics. More broadly, this framework provides a general approach for studying longitudinal network dynamics through the estimation of network-generating mechanisms over time.

raw_data.title: A Computational Model Captures Orexin-Dependent Modulation of Memory Consolidation.
raw_data.abstract: Hippocampal sharp-wave ripple (SWR) events occur during post-experience rest and sleep and play a significant role in memory consolidation. Recent ex vivo studies have found orexin-driven neuromodulatory effects on SWR parameters and proposed that they can influence memory consolidation. Additionally, behavioral studies demonstrate contradictory results regarding orexinergic effects on memory acquisition depending on task structure and intervention time. This inconsistency, along with the diffuse spread of orexin receptors (OXR) in the CA1 and CA3 hippocampus, challenges theoretical interpretation of orexinergic effects on memory. To reconcile this problem, we propose a rate-based model linking orexinergic tone-dependent SWR statistics to memory performance. The model combines an encoding module whose gain scales with the global orexinergic tone with a consolidation module driven by OX2R-specific replay dynamics. The model is based on a plasticity rule that considers SWR events as the unit of induction. Therefore, weight change requires sufficient replay content and depolarizing drive. We observed that, depending on the task structure, encoding-dominant learning benefits discrimination as the orexin drive increases. Consolidation-dominant learning shows a non-monotonic relationship with an internal optimum level of orexinergic tone. This interaction highlights that stronger truncation at higher receptor engagement shortens memory replay and reduces the efficacy of the consolidation process. The model predicts that the optimal regime depends on task complexity reflected in sequence length. Together, these results demonstrate how task demands determine whether increased orexinergic drive enhances or impairs effective consolidation and SWR-dependent replay in the hippocampus.

raw_data.title: ASC specks and α-synuclein amplify microglial NLRP3 inflammasome activation and co-localize with Lewy body pathology
raw_data.abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of several chronic neurodegenerative disorders, including Parkinson's disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies, and is closely associated with microglial activation. The inflammasome adaptor protein apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a caspase activation and recruitment domain (ASC) undergoes oligomerization upon inflammasome activation, resulting in the formation of ASC specks. These structures are recognized by microglia as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), thereby promoting inflammatory signaling. Recent studies have demonstrated that extracellular ASC specks associate with amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}), and that uptake of ASC-A{beta} composites by microglia amplifies pro-inflammatory responses. Although ASC specks have also been shown to potentiate -synuclein (Syn) preformed fibril-induced pathology, their interaction with monomeric Syn and their effects on inflammasome activation remain poorly understood. Here, we co-stimulated murine SIM-A9 microglia with ASC-Syn assemblies and evaluated their effects on NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Electron microscopy revealed a close association between ASC fibrils and Syn monomers. Exposure of microglia to ASC-Syn enhanced NLRP3 inflammasome activation, as evidenced by increased ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activation, and secretion of IL-1{beta} and IL-18, when compared to ASC or Syn alone. In addition, immunohistochemical analyses of post mortem brain tissue from patients with dementia with Lewy bodies demonstrated ASC expression in regions exhibiting Syn pathology and showed ASC co-localization with Syn within Lewy bodies. Collectively, these findings identify ASC-Syn assemblies as potent amplifiers of NLRP3 inflammasome signaling and suggest a mechanism through which they may contribute to sustained neuroinflammation in synucleinopathies.

raw_data.title: A Bayesian approach to volumetric analysis in rare neurodegenerative disorders
raw_data.abstract: Identifying regional brain atrophy is critical for understanding neurodegenerative disorders. Traditionally, group comparisons rely on frequentist statistics, utilising $p$-values and point estimates that offer limited characterization of uncertainty. Bayesian methods provide an alternative by estimating effect sizes and credible intervals while incorporating prior knowledge and uncertainty. This study evaluated the feasibility of Bayesian hierarchical modelling to assess regional brain atrophy in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy (PSP) and Corticobasal Syndrome (CBS) compared to healthy controls. Participants meeting diagnostic criteria for CBS or PSP, together with healthy controls, were recruited from the Cambridge Centre for Parkinson-plus. Grey matter volume, cortical thickness, and subcortical volumes were derived using FreeSurfer for 210 cortical and 36 subcortical regions defined by the Human Brainnetome Atlas. Participants with PSP were classified into Richardson syndrome (PSP-RS), corticobasal syndrome variant (PSP-CBS), frontal variant (PSP-F), and other presentations (PSP-Other). Bayesian hierarchical ANOVA models with appropriate priors were used to estimate group differences. Regions of practical equivalence (ROPE) were calculated to assess evidence of meaningful group effects. A total of 428 people were included (113 PSP-RS, 30 PSP-CBS, 23 PSP-Other, 19 PSP-F, 81 CBS, and 162 healthy controls). For grey matter volume, there was evidence of whole brain volume loss compared to controls for all disease groups except PSP-Other, which showed evidence of no difference. For cortical thickness, there was evidence of global cortical thinning in CBS compared to controls, but for no other group. For subcortical volume all groups showed evidence of volume loss compared to controls. Patterns of regional atrophy were identified in keeping with previous literature, with the largest effect observed in the left pre-motor thalamus (30\% reduction in CBS). There was greater loss of subcortical volume in PSP-RS compared to other PSP subgroups. Bayesian hierarchical modelling provides a feasible framework for quantifying regional brain atrophy, with interpretable effect size estimates and uncertainty measures. This approach complements conventional statistical methods, particularly in the assessment of rare neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders.

raw_data.title: Using the aperiodic slope across learning to predict sleep-based memory consolidation
raw_data.abstract: Homeostatic mechanisms adjust synaptic strengths to regulate neuronal activity across wake-sleep cycles. Although sleep supports memory consolidation, limited research has explored how sleep-induced homeostatic changes influence memory outcomes in humans. The EEG-derived aperiodic slope (1/f) could be a candidate measure of homeostatic memory processes through its reflection of neural excitation-inhibition balance. In this study, 27 participants learned object-word pairs, and completed an immediate recognition test before either a nap or equivalent wakeful period. Resting-state EEG was recorded, both before and after learning and the interval, to derive changes in aperiodic slope values. A delayed recognition test then assessed whether changes in the aperiodic slope (i.e., homeostatic activity) across learning and the interval predicted memory accuracy and N400 amplitude, an index of stimulus expectancy and recognition. Our study found evidence to suggest homeostatic renormalisation, for the nap condition only, indicated by a shift towards inhibition across sleep which was inversely related to the slope change across learning. Although the aperiodic slope change across the nap and wake intervals did not predict delayed memory accuracy, a shift towards inhibition during learning was beneficial for memory accuracy, only in the nap condition. Similarly, a shift towards inhibition across learning, followed by a shift towards excitation in the nap condition, predicted reduced N400 amplitudes. This suggests that homeostatic renormalisation across the nap influenced model updating and stimulus expectancy. This study provides evidence for a link between synaptic homeostatic processes and memory consolidation, emphasising the importance of encoding-related aperiodic activity in this relationship.

raw_data.title: Inferotemporal cortex stimulation is perceived before its onset
raw_data.abstract: Neural response latency measures when stimulus-evoked activity becomes detectable, but it does not reveal when the brain assigns the causal contribution of that activity to events in the external world. We define this temporal adjustment as projected delay and measure it in the macaque inferotemporal cortex using optogenetic stimulation and behavior. Two rhesus macaques performed a cortical perturbation detection task in which a visual masker appeared at different times relative to stimulation. Detection was selectively impaired when the masker began 200 ms before stimulation. We then tested this timing using Perceptography, a method that optimizes image perturbations to mimic stimulation-evoked visual events. Image perturbations presented 200 ms before stimulation elicited higher false-alarm rates than perturbations presented at stimulation onset. Here, we show that stimulation-evoked visual events in inferotemporal cortex depend preferentially on visual information originating approximately 200 ms before the cortical perturbation. This projected delay exceeds typical inferotemporal response latencies and suggests temporally extended readout mechanisms relevant to causal models of visual perception and the timing of cortical visual prostheses.

raw_data.title: The genetic landscape of myotonic dystrophy type 1: insights from nearly one million genomes.
raw_data.abstract: Myotonic Dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a multisystem disorder caused by CTG repeat expansions in the dystrophia myotonica protein kinase (DMPK) gene. Current prevalence estimates of 1 in 3,000-8,000 have traditionally relied on clinically ascertained and geographically restricted cohorts, underestimating population burden and failing to capture ancestry diversity. Using large-scale whole-genome sequencing (WGS) datasets, we aimed to identify DMPK repeat expansions across nearly one million participants, define their ancestry-specific distribution, and evaluate associated clinical phenotypes, with particular focus on cardiac manifestations and early-onset cataracts. We analysed WGS participants from three cohorts: Genomics England (n = 80,110), UK Biobank (n = 490,086), and the All of Us Research Program (n = 414,830). DMPK repeat lengths were estimated using ExpansionHunter. Alleles were classified as Normal (≤37 repeats), Intermediate (38-49 repeats), or Pathogenic (≥50 repeats). Genetic ancestry was assigned using cohort-specific methods. Linked health record data assessed cardiac phenotypes in UK Biobank and early-onset cataracts in Genomics England and UK Biobank. Across all cohorts (n = 985,026), pathogenic DMPK repeat expansions were identified in 645 individuals (0.07%; ∼1 in 1,527), a prevalence two-to-five times higher than previous estimates. Most expansions occurred in those of European ancestry, although expansions were detected across all groups, including up to 1 in 6,693 African and Asian ancestry. In UK Biobank, individuals with a pathogenic expansion had increased odds of any cardiac diagnosis (odds ratio [OR]: 2.06, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.58-2.67; p = 5.8×108) and greater cardiac diagnostic burden (risk ratio 2.46, CI: 1.92-3.15; p = 1.6×10-13). Conduction abnormalities-particularly atrioventricular and left bundle-branch block, atrial fibrillation, and flutter-showed the strongest association with expansion status (OR: 4.86, CI: 3.38-6.79; p = 2.7×10-18). No sex differences were observed among those with a DMPK expansion, although male sex was independently associated with conduction disease in the overall population. Approximately one-in-ten individuals with pathogenic expansions had a cataract diagnosis before age 55. Most individuals with an expansion had no prior DM1 diagnosis, highlighting the value of systematic genetic testing in these phenotypes to improve diagnosis, shorten the diagnostic interval, and mitigate harm. By integrating WGS data from nearly one million individuals, this study refines understanding of the population distribution and clinical consequences of DMPK repeat expansions, revealing a reservoir of undiagnosed and potentially untreated multisystemic disease. These findings support routine inclusion of DMPK analysis within specified cardiac and ophthalmic diagnostic pathways to enable earlier detection.

raw_data.title: Synaptic input architecture of visual cortical neurons revealed by large-scale synapse imaging without backpropagating action potentials
raw_data.abstract: How neurons integrate thousands of synaptic inputs to compute sharply tuned outputs is a critical question in sensory information processing. To answer this question, it is essential to record the location and activity of synaptic inputs in vivo. However, back-propagating action potential (BAP) calcium signals invade dendrites and spines, making accurate recording of spine responses difficult. In this study, we first developed a new method to record spine calcium responses without BAP signals. Using this method, we performed large-scale imaging of visually evoked spine activity from layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons and revealed three patterns of dendritic functional architectures of synaptic inputs: dendrites with clusters of spines of similar responses, dendrites with spines of diverse responses, and dendrites with spines where the majority of them show no visual response. Our model suggests that only a small fraction of spines on dendrites of clustered architectures are sufficient to generate sharply tuned output.

raw_data.title: Robust brain inspired prediction of speech recognition accuracy across many words, voices, and natural background sounds
raw_data.abstract:
Although humans generally excel at recognizing speech in noisy natural environments, performance varies widely due to differences in the background acoustics and individual talker attributes such as voice quality, intonation, and pitch. The underlying neural and acoustic factors of this perceptual variability remain elusive, making it an unresolved challenge to predict when speech recognition will succeed or fail. Here, we characterize human speech recognition across a wide range of natural conditions using speech spoken by 326 diverse male and female talkers of multiple ages embedded in 33 unique background noises. Across this vast soundscape, speech recognition is strongly driven by the spectrum and modulation statistics of the noise. Yet, articulatory speech features - including fundamental and formant frequencies - exert categorically distinct modulatory effects on recognition accuracy across the talkers age and gender, and specific words. This perceptual variability is captured by a low-dimensional statistical representation of sounds based on computations that emulate intermediate stages of sound processing and feature extraction in auditory midbrain. A model utilizing these sound summary statistics accurately predicts individual listeners single-trial recognition behavior, accounting for performance variance across individual voices, words, and backgrounds. Thus, speech-in-noise perception across diverse natural conditions relies largely on a simple set of spectrotemporal summary statistics known to be represented by central neural populations.

Significance StatementAlthough humans can easily maintain conversations amidst environmental noise and voice variations, this capacity is severely degraded by hearing impairment and challenges modern speech recognition technologies. This study evaluates human speech recognition across a broad spectrum of environmental noises and diverse speaker demographics. We show that a brain-inspired auditory representation of sounds extracts critical statistical sound features driving human behavior, precisely predicting variations in perceptual accuracy across distinct voices, words, and environmental backgrounds.

raw_data.title: Mechanistic simulation identifies predictive dose-dependent biomarkers of propofol anesthesia
raw_data.abstract: Understanding how receptor-level modulation reorganizes large-scale brain circuits remains a central challenge in neuropharmacology. Here we introduce a multiscale mechanistic model with explicit core-matrix thalamocortical architecture to examine how propofol reorganizes brainwide activity from individual receptors to systems-level circuits. Crucially, the model did not involve machine learning or statistical fitting to pre-existing anesthesia data. We use the model to simulate the multi-scale effects of propofol, which range from modulation of individual synaptic conductances to widespread alterations of neural spiking, field potentials, and coherence. Without requiring any training on task-specific data, our simulation of sensory processing in a standard auditory oddball paradigm matches independent data from anesthetized and awake behaving macaques. The same simulation, unmodified, also reproduces changes to functional connectivity in anesthetized humans, exhibiting selective attenuation of matrix thalamocortical loops relative to core loops. Most importantly, the simulation identified a previously unknown biomarker of propofol concentration: elevated residual inter-stimulus cortical activity. This dose-dependent biomarker was subsequently confirmed in empirical macaque data, where it had previously gone unnoticed. This simulation-first discovery, arising from mechanistic circuit dynamics rather than statistical comparison of clinical populations, serves as an illustrative example of a broader generative framework that can translate receptor-level modulation into circuit-scale biomarkers with potential applications across predictive neuropharmacology.

raw_data.title: Pharmacokinetic properties of Ogerin and its regulation of post-ischemia signaling in mice
raw_data.abstract: Ogerin, a positive regulator of GPR68, reduces infarct volume and attenuates blood-brain barrier (BBB) leakage post transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO). These data support the potential use of Ogerin for ischemic protection. For therapeutic interventions, tissue distribution, kinetics, and brain penetration are important characteristics for a compound. For these reasons, we performed liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis of Ogerin in mice. At 3 hours following intraperitoneal (IP) injection, liver exhibited highest level of Ogerin among all major organs assessed. We further analyzed time-dependent changes in Ogerin concentration in serum following intravenous delivery. Brain Ogerin level was ~140 ng/g at 2 hour and ~0.06ng/g at 24 hours. The brain-to-serum ratio of Ogerin was ~0.6 at 5 hr. To determine the effect of Ogerin on signaling, we collected samples 24 hours after tMCAO with or without Ogerin delivered and performed Western blotting. Consistent with the diminished level of Ogerin in brain at 24 hour, tMCAO increased similar changes in phosphorylation of PKA substrates and PKC substrates in vehicle- and Ogerin-treated groups. The pharmacokinetic data suggests that Ogerin is effective mainly during acute hours after injection. This finding generates important insights on the design of effective protocol for Ogerin delivery to potentiate GPR68 function in vivo.

raw_data.title: Lateral recurrence dynamically refines visual representations for task performance
raw_data.abstract: Recurrent connections are pervasive in visual cortex, and visual representations evolve as recurrent processing unfolds. Yet the mechanism underlying this temporal transformation remains poorly understood. To address this question, we trained recurrent convolutional networks on face and object recognition and tested them on a parametric stimulus set in which category, identity, and pose were systematically varied. This design isolates how lateral recurrence reshapes neural-population representational geometry and single-unit tuning across recurrent timesteps. Within the trained domain, recurrence increased the separability between identities in deeper layers, while leaving the non-trained domain representations largely unchanged. Gating lateral weights abolished the across-timestep gain in trained-domain identity decoding, demonstrating that lateral recurrence drives this refinement. At the single-unit level, recurrence strengthened the correlation between each unit's category preference and its within-domain identity sensitivity, providing a unit-level mechanism for the population-level changes. These results identify lateral recurrence as a dynamic mechanism for refining learned representational structure within a fixed neural population, yielding testable predictions for time-resolved recordings in domain-selective cortex.

raw_data.title: A network model of path control
raw_data.abstract: We present a network model that enables a navigating agent to shape the spatial and temporal structure of its paths through its environment. The model is inspired by the insect fan-shaped body. In it, a recurrent neural network receives an input that encodes an agent's velocity vector. Meanwhile, network activity determines the setpoint of a control loop that influences this velocity vector through motor outputs. The network thus guides future movement using memory of past movement. We illustrate how the network's dynamics determine the trajectory features it extracts to produce the setpoint. We then relate the joint dynamics of network activity and the agent's velocity vector to the structure of the resulting paths. This network can produce paths suitable for different forms of exploration. It can also stabilize movements initiated by lower-level systems. Our analyses illustrate how recurrent neural dynamics and memory can shape behavior when embedded in closed loops.

raw_data.title: Projection-defined ventral tegmental area neurons exhibit distinct molecular adaptations during acute fentanyl withdrawal
raw_data.abstract: Opioid use disorder (OUD) remains a major public health concern, with potent synthetic opioids driving overdose deaths. Understanding how synthetic opioids like fentanyl alter brain circuits to promote persistent use is critical for advancing OUD treatment. The ventral tegmental area (VTA), which projects to several other brain regions including prefrontal cortex (PFC), nucleus accumbens (NAc) and amygdala (Amy), contributes to both the euphoric and dysphoric phases of OUD. Projection target influences the baseline properties and opioid-induced neuroadaptations of VTA neurons, yet less is known about the molecular adaptations that occur across distinct VTA projections during spontaneous opioid withdrawal. Here, we investigated transcriptional responses to acute spontaneous fentanyl withdrawal in projection-defined VTA neurons. Following chronic fentanyl exposure and 24h of spontaneous withdrawal in male and female mice, we sequenced ribosome-associated RNA from VTA neurons projecting to PFC, NAc, or Amy. We found that fentanyl withdrawal produced divergent transcriptional adaptations in VTA neurons projecting to PFC compared with VTA-NAc and VTA-Amy neurons, whereas adaptations in VTA-NAc and VTA-Amy neurons were more concordant. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified fentanyl-responsive modules across VTA projections, with gene ontology analysis linking these modules to distinct biological processes. We further used regulatory enrichment analysis to identify candidate transcriptional regulators associated with fentanyl-responsive co-expression modules. Together, our data demonstrate that VTA neurons undergo distinct molecular adaptations during fentanyl withdrawal based on their projection target, providing new insight into molecular mechanisms relevant to OUD.

raw_data.title: Learning Interpretable Switching Dynamics in Shared Neural-Behavioral Latent Space
raw_data.abstract: Modern recording technologies enable simultaneous measurement of high-dimensional neural activity and rich behavioral variables, creating both an opportunity and a modeling challenge: identifying the shared latent structure that mediates the brain-behavior relationship and the underlying dynamics through which it evolves across behavioral states. Existing approaches focus on different parts of this challenge: shared representation learning methods identify neural-behavioral subspaces but typically do not model dynamical structure, while dynamical models capture temporal variation and discrete state transitions in neural activity, but do not explicitly disentangle shared neural-behavioral structure from modality-specific variability. We introduce Switching Shared Latent Dynamics (SSLD), a unified framework that learns a latent representation shared between neural activity and behavior and endows this shared space with nonlinear switching recurrent dynamics to reflect the hypothesis that behaviorally relevant neural representations exhibit structured dynamical changes across behavioral states. Complementary private latent variables capture modality-specific variability, providing a window into neural activity that does not directly interact with behavior. We evaluate SSLD on a simulated dataset and four diverse experimental datasets spanning species, brain regions, and recording modalities: monkey motor and premotor cortex during reaching, somatosensory cortex during a bump task, widefield calcium imaging across mouse dorsal cortex during (a) self-initiated decision-making and (b) spontaneous movements. Across all four datasets, SSLD accurately reconstructs neural and behavioral signals, recovers discrete states in the dynamics that align with experimentally defined behavioral epochs, and isolates behaviorally-relevant neural information in the shared latent while preserving private neural variability. Ablations confirm that shared representation learning, behavioral supervision, and switching dynamics each contribute to performance. SSLD offers an interpretable approach to modeling shared neural-behavioral dynamics that complements ongoing efforts toward foundation models for neuroscience.

raw_data.title: Moving object generates topographic responses in the majority of entorhinal neurons
raw_data.abstract: Vision is crucial in generating a complex array of responses in rodents during spatial exploration and in humans during memory tasks. These tasks involve other variables too, e.g. multisensory cues in rodents and complex memories in humans. Further, there are major differences between the medial and lateral entorhinal cortical (MEC and LEC) functional cell types. To understand the contribution of purely visual information to entorhinal responses, we presented a simple, moving vertical bar of light to head-fixed mice, without any task or reward. Surprisingly, 66% (2391/3601) of the MEC broad spiking neurons were significantly modulated by the bar position on the screen. Visual tuning in MEC had a pronounced dorsoventral topography --the tuning strength dropped from 79% in the dorsal most quartile to 40% in the ventral most quartile. Unlike major differences in spatial and other codes between MEC and LEC during free foraging experiments, LEC cells showed very similar visual tuning (392/606, 65%), including the dorso-ventral gradient in LEC5. Additionally, the majority of putative interneurons, from MEC as well as LEC, showed similar, widespread visual tuning, unlike spatial tasks. Neurons also encoded the object motion direction (naso-temporal vs. temporo-nasal visual motion) with changes in mean rate, tuning strength and/or tuning location. Such directional nature of visual tuning indicates significant history-dependence or sequence encoding. Consistently, replacing the continuous motion by randomly flashing bar of light abolished bar-tuning in two-thirds of continuous bar-tuned cells and substantially altered tuning in the rest. These results reveal the contribution of purely visual inputs in generating anatomically organized responses in the majority of entorhinal neurons. The prevalence and similarity of visual tuning across all layers of MEC as well as LEC exceeds that of other known functional cell types (like grid cells in MEC or egocentric object tuning/time-cells in LEC) during spatial navigation tasks and could be foundational in understanding entorhinal complexity.

raw_data.title: Sex Differences in Human Subcortical Anatomy are Robust and Replicable in Adulthood, Already Evident Prepubertally, and Aligned with Sex Chromosomal and Gonadal Influences
raw_data.abstract: The existence and mechanistic bases of sex effects on human subcortical anatomy remain unclear. To address these gaps, we combined structural neuroimaging of sex differences in subcortical volume and shape across three independent cohorts (combined N=2,886) with neuroimaging maps of sex chromosomal and endocrine effects from three clinical cohorts (combined N=313, including sex chromosome aneuploidies and isolated gonadotropin-releasing hormone deficiency). We found that human subcortical anatomy shows focal sex differences of moderate-strong effect size during young adulthood (male-biased surface area overlying lateral/ventral putamen and pallidum, nucleus accumbens, ventral posterior complex of thalamus, anterior hippocampus, and medial and central nuclei of amygdala; female-biased surface area overlying caudate head, posterior/dorsal pallidum, mediodorsal, lateral dorsal, lateral geniculate, and medial geniculate nuclei of thalamus, posterior hippocampus, and basolateral and lateral nuclei of amygdala). These regional sex differences show strong within-sample reproducibility at modest sample sizes (N[≥]200) and are replicable in a fully independent mid-adulthood cohort. Adult subcortical sex differences are already evident in nascent form by pre/early puberty (age 9 years), and the same holds for cortical sex differences. Comparison with neuroimaging data from rare disorder cohorts reveals a statistically significant spatial and directional congruence of subcortical sex differences with the anatomical effects of X-chromosome dosage in the striatum and effects of testicular hormones in the amygdala. Our findings provide a reference map for the fine-grained spatial patterning of sex differences in adult subcortical shape, demonstrating its replicability, establishment before pubertal progression, and spatial concordance with potentially causal sex chromosomal and gonadal effects.

raw_data.title: Neuron types and distribution of a Drosophila driver line collection
raw_data.abstract: Cell type designations label uniquely-identifiable groups of related cells that typically function in similar ways. Cell types divide the Drosophila melanogaster central nervous system into functional units, but remain challenging to target and identify. Previously we generated a driver line and image resource for targeting many neuron types (Meissner et al., 2025). Here we improve on identifying the targeted neurons by automated searching against electron microscopy datasets and manual scoring of search results to add 6,368 annotations across 1,772 driver lines in the collection. These annotations provide a potential training resource for future search algorithms. We then estimate the number of cell types and thus the fraction of the central nervous system labeled by the collection as a whole.

raw_data.title: Neuronal sex identity shapes social buffering of defensive freezing behaviour in fruit flies
raw_data.abstract: Sex differences are pervasive across the animal kingdom1,2, shaped by reproductive strategies, ecological roles, and physiological demands. Neurobiological studies have largely focused on sex differences in reproduction and aggression3,4, leaving understudied how sex shapes other survival-relevant behaviours such as responses to predatory threats. Previous work in vertebrates uncovered sex differences in individual defence responses deployed by rats5 and in social modulation of freezing responses in zebrafish6. The origin of these differences and their potential underlying neuronal circuitry remain however unknown. Here we characterise defensive responses to a visual threat of female and male fruit flies tested alone and in groups. Individually, defensive responses are comparable across sex, with similar freezing levels and moderately increased escape responses in males. In groups, however, we uncovered strong sex differences in freezing as males show consistently shorter freezing bouts, reflecting a stronger social buffering effect than in females. Using a generalised linear mixed model, we demonstrate that the shorter freezes of male flies, when tested in groups, are not explained by well-known locomotor differences between sexes7,8. Although males move more and faster, generating stronger social motion cues that mediate the "safety in numbers" effect in female flies9,10, their response to the surrounding motion is not increased. We further identify the nervous system as the source of this sex-dimorphic behaviour by feminising males through pan-neuronal ectopic expression of transformer, a key regulator of the cell-autonomous sex-differentiation pathway. Finally, we ruled out the visual projection neurons, lobula columnar neurons 11 (LC11), detectors of social motion10, as the source of the neuronal-sex differences observed. This study identifies a neuronal origin of sex differences in socially modulated behaviour that extends beyond sex-specific behavioural modules or locomotor function, important to understand differential impact on survival upon threat across sexes.

raw_data.title: Encephalitic alphavirus infection reduces neurite outgrowth and downregulates Rho GTPase pathways in human iPSC-derived neurospheres
raw_data.abstract: Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus (VEEV) is a re-emerging neurotropic arbovirus, which affects the developing human brain, potentially leading to miscarriage, stillbirth, or long-term neurological sequelae. Currently, the mechanisms underlying these sequelae remain largely elusive. Using human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurospheres as a model for brain development, we show that both human neurons and glial cells are susceptible to VEEV infection. Microscopy-based quantification reveals that VEEV impairs neurite outgrowth in the human neurospheres. To mechanistically assess these observations, we performed multi-omics analyses of VEEV-infected neurospheres and demonstrate translational shutoff including downregulation of Rho GTPase pathways. The transcriptional and proteome profile is indicative of reduced actin cytoskeleton dynamics and consequently migratory defects of cells in the neurospheres. Shotgun secretomics moreover revealed downmodulation of neurite outgrowth associated proteins including midkine (MDK), amyloid-beta precursor protein (APP) and microtubule-associated protein 1B (MAP1B). Our findings reveal mechanistic insights into how VEEV infection impairs neuronal development and demonstrate that neurospheres are a powerful platform for assessing teratogenic effects of viruses on brain development.

raw_data.title: An AI-Enabled Translational Drug Discovery Framework for NALCN Channelopathy: From High-Throughput Screening to Therapeutic Candidate
raw_data.abstract: Background: More than 90% of rare diseases lack an approved therapy, partly reflecting economic barriers in developing treatments for small patient populations. A common bottleneck is costly and resource-intensive hit-to-lead prioritization. Congenital contractures of the limbs and face, hypotonia, and developmental delay (CLIFAHDD) is an ultra-rare neurodevelopmental disease often caused by de novo gain-of-function variants in the sodium leak channel NALCN, with no approved treatments. Methods: We developed a cost and resource-efficient, AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic high-throughput screening (HTS), structural biology foundation models for hit-to-lead prioritization, and orthogonal experimental validation. We applied this framework for drug repurposing to identify NALCN inhibitors as therapeutic candidates for CLIFAHDD. We screened ~1,200 approved drugs using a fluorescence-based membrane potential assay in doxycycline-inducible HEK293 cells stably expressing the NALCN channelosome. Boltz-2 modeling predicted binding affinity and mode to prioritize hits. Lead repurposing candidates were selected by a multidisciplinary expert review panel. Lead candidates were evaluated using patch-clamp electrophysiology in HEK293 cells expressing wild-type or CLIFAHDD-associated NALCN variants, primary mouse hippocampal neurons, and a C. elegans NALCN gain-of-function model. Results: HTS identified 11 candidate NALCN inhibitors. Boltz-2 prioritized candidates based on predicted binding affinity and predicted binding within the NALCN pore, consistent with a direct pore-blocking mechanism. Aprepitant emerged as the lead candidate after multidisciplinary evaluation based on its predicted mechanism, pharmacologic properties, blood-brain barrier penetration, established safety profile, and regulatory approval in children and adults. Patch-clamp electrophysiology confirmed partial inhibition of NALCN-mediated sodium leak currents in HEK293 cells (IC50;=2.22 M), with comparable potency against Cav3.1 (IC50=1.63 M). In primary mouse hippocampal neurons, aprepitant reduced sodium leak currents, hyperpolarized resting membrane potential, and decreased spontaneous firing. Aprepitant rescued hyperlocomotor and dystonic phenotypes in a C. elegans gain-of-function NALCN model. There was notable concordance between AI-predicted hits, phenotypic screening hits, and experimental validation. Conclusion: These findings identify aprepitant as a lead therapeutic candidate for CLIFAHDD, and establish an AI-enabled translational drug discovery framework integrating phenotypic screening, structural modeling, and experimental validation for NALCN channelopathies. This scalable and resource-conscious strategy may accelerate hit-to-lead prioritization and drug discovery for rare and ultra-rare diseases lacking effective therapies.

raw_data.title: Microstructural heterogeneity of white-matter aging and its age-dependent coupling to cognition
raw_data.abstract: Brain white matter (WM) microstructure undergoes extensive changes with age, yet the regional and cellular heterogeneity of age-related WM alterations and their impact on cognition remain unclear. Leveraging Neurite Orientation Dispersion and Density Imaging (NODDI), an advanced microstructural modelling to capture specific WM cellular properties, we investigated age-dependent relationships between advanced microstructural markers and cognitive performance, indexed by six cognitive domains derived from principal component analysis. Using a suite of standard diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and NODDI techniques in eighty-six cognitively normal adults (Young: n=33, Older: n=53), we show that age group differences are widespread across whole brain white matter, with converging region-based and voxel-level evidence implicating commissural, association, and limbic pathways. Older adults exhibited significant and widespread reductions in global fractional anisotropy (FA) and neurite density index (NDI), concomitant with increases in mean diffusivity (MD), orientation density index (ODI), and free water fraction (FWF). Critically, age moderated WM-cognition associations in a domain- and tract-specific manner: younger adults exhibited stronger coupling between commissural and association tract microstructure and language and visual memory, whereas older adults showed greater dependence on projection and limbic tracts for executive and language function. The observed age-dependent coupling between specific microstructural metrics and cognition underscores the value of advanced diffusion models for capturing heterogeneity in brain aging, reveals age-specific biomarkers of cognitive health. These patterns align with phylogenetic and ontogenetic patterns of white matter vulnerability in callosal, long-range association, and limbic pathways, and suggest cellular specificity in white matter changes associated with cognitive decline.

raw_data.abstract: Exposure of pregnant women to toxic metals is an environmental health issue associated with pregnancy complications. Advancing our biological understanding of this problem and mitigating its adverse effects have been challenged by the ethical constraints of human participant research during pregnancy. Here we present a microphysiological system to experimentally simulate and investigate human placental exposure to environmental metals in maternal circulation. An in vitro analogue of the maternal–fetal interface and its dynamic tissue-specific environment are constructed using primary human placental cells grown in a microfluidic device. Using cadmium as a representative toxicant, we show how this system can be used to model the human placental barrier subjected to the flow of cadmium-containing maternal blood and its adverse biological responses and impaired tissue function. Through mechanistic investigation of maternal-to-fetal cadmium transport in this model, we reveal that efflux membrane transporters expressed by trophoblasts may play a protective role against cadmium-induced toxicity. Finally, we demonstrate the potential use of the microphysiological system for discovering metabolic biomarkers for detection and monitoring of cadmium-induced placental dysfunction.

raw_data.abstract: A successful infection requires pathogens to recognize the specific host environment in order to reprogram their physiology accordingly. One major way in which eukaryotic cells sense their surroundings is via G-Protein Coupled Receptors (GPCRs), which share a seven-transmembrane architecture and G-protein-mediated downstream signaling. While mammalian GPCRs are well-characterized and represent important drug targets, their fungal counterparts remain poorly understood. Here we uncover a GPCR-based mechanism that allows the corn pathogen Ustilago maydis to sense whether it has entered plant tissue. During infection, the fungus secretes the protein Pit2, which is cleaved by host apoplastic cysteine proteases, releasing a peptide ligand ‘hidden’ within the protein core. This ligand activates the fungal GPCR Gpe1, thus promoting fungal proliferation after initial host penetration. We elucidate the crystal structure of Pit2 and model the complex formed by Gpe1 and the Pit2-derived peptide. Structure-guided mutational analysis supports that disrupting this interaction reduces fungal virulence. The Gpe1/Pit2 system is conserved in related fungal species, with co-evolutionary signatures apparently preserving receptor-ligand specificity. Furthermore, this system shows mechanistic similarities to mammalian receptors, suggesting an evolutionary link between fungal and mammalian GPCRs.

raw_data.abstract: Cas9 is a metal-dependent nuclease used for genome editing across diverse cells and organisms exhibiting distinct ionic environments, yet how metal ions regulate its catalytic function, and consequently its editing efficiency remains unclear. Here, molecular simulations, Markov state models, and mixed quantum–classical approaches reveal that divalent metals promote activation of the catalytic HNH domain through formation of a divalent metal-binding pocket (DBP) at the HNH–RuvC interface. This cryptic pocket emerges dynamically during HNH activation and is supported by NMR measurements revealing metal-dependent structural perturbations within the HNH–L2 region. Mutations targeting the DBP disrupt HNH activation and impair the coupled catalytic activity of both nucleases, identifying the pocket as a key regulator of Cas9’s metal-dependent activity. Together with quantum–classical simulations revealing distinct catalytic behaviours among divalent metals, these findings uncover an ion-dependent regulatory mechanism in Cas9 with insights for genome editing across diverse biological environments.

raw_data.abstract: During replication-coupled DNA interstrand cross-link (ICL) repair, fork reversal is thought to enable the Fanconi anemia (FA) pathway to resolve the ICL through nucleolytic incisions. The resulting regressed arm of the reversed fork undergoes extensive nucleolytic resection that may facilitate completion of replication. Despite the importance of these remodeling events, their regulation remains poorly understood. Here, we use cell-free Xenopus egg extracts and human cells to investigate reversed fork processing during ICL repair by the FA pathway. We find that the ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) kinase is activated concomitantly with fork reversal and promotes resection of reversed fork intermediates. ATM enhances chromatin recruitment of DNA2, which acts alongside EXO1 to resect reversed forks formed during ICL repair. Moreover, inhibition of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) leads to ATM hyperactivation, accelerated reversed fork processing, and accumulation of aberrant end-joining products, implying that PP2A restrains ATM signaling to limit reversed fork resection. Taken together, this work identifies reversed forks as substrates for ATM activation and reveals a phospho-regulatory circuit that controls reversed fork processing.

raw_data.abstract: Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) are short, synthetic nucleic acids that bind to complementary RNA sequences and alter gene expression, making them versatile therapeutic agents. Here, we identify transcription termination windows of protein-coding genes as previously unrecognised targets for ASOs. We show that ASOs can act on nascent RNA synthesised downstream of the annotated genes, leading to a pronounced decrease in the corresponding mRNA levels. These downstream of gene ASOs (DG-ASOs) induce RNase H1-dependent cleavage, impairing mRNA 3’ end processing, directing the unprocessed mRNAs for exosome-dependent degradation and creating early entry points in the nascent RNA for the XRN2 exonuclease termination factor. Altogether, we show that termination windows are genuine ASO targets which can be exploited to suppress gene expression. Importantly, we also reveal an underappreciated source of off-target effects which may arise from ASOs binding downstream of genes. Our findings indicate the necessity to expand ASO design and off-target assessment guidelines to include termination window sequences, thereby improving therapeutic efficacy and safety.

title_zh: 靶向转录终止窗口的反义寡核苷酸干扰mRNA 3'末端加工并降低基因表达
recommendation_text: 该研究揭示了反义寡核苷酸（ASO）的全新作用靶点——转录终止窗口，通过靶向基因下游新生RNA（DG-ASO）诱导RNase H1依赖的切割，破坏mRNA 3'端加工，从而显著降低基因表达。这一发现不仅拓展了ASO疗法的设计维度，为精准调控致病基因提供了新策略，也对神经科学中基因表达操控（如通过ASO敲低神经元或胶质细胞特定基因）具有重要方法学意义。其机制独立于传统ASO靶向成熟mRNA的路径，可能为神经系统疾病治疗带来更高效的工具。
reasoning: 该研究揭示ASO靶向转录终止窗口调控基因表达的新机制，属分子生物学范畴，但ASO技术广泛用于神经科学基因功能研究与治疗，对神经科学有重要推动价值。
feature_angle: 反义寡核苷酸可靶向转录终止窗口，通过干扰mRNA 3'端加工抑制基因表达，同时揭示ASO疗法中一个被忽视的脱靶效应来源。
key_strength: 鉴定出蛋白编码基因下游转录终止窗口是ASO的全新作用靶点，阐明RNase H1切割、外切体降解及XRN2提前介入的分子机制，对ASO设计与安全性评估具有直接指导意义。
key_limitation: 机制主要基于细胞系实验，缺乏动物体内递送与毒性验证；DG-ASO对基因表达的抑制效率与经典靶向策略的定量比较不足，且终止窗口序列的预测规则尚未系统建立。
target_audience: 核酸药物开发与ASO设计研究者、RNA加工与转录终止领域学者、基因表达调控及系统生物学研究人员。
crossover_value: 神经科学 increasingly 依赖基因表达操控来研究神经环路与疾病机制，ASO是重要工具。该研究提出的DG-ASO策略可提高基因敲低效率，尤其适用于难以靶向的转录本，为在体神经科学研究提供更精准的调控手段，并可能推动神经系统疾病（如亨廷顿病、肌萎缩侧索硬化）的ASO疗法优化。

raw_data.abstract: The functional integrity of a mammalian chromosome depends on its long-term co-evolution with species-specific nuclear environment. How chromosomes co-adapt with their native environment to define 3D architecture and transcription remains unclear, largely due to a lack of experimental models that dissect this co-evolution. Here, we report cross-species chromosome substitution (CROSS), a method enabling stable, scarless replacement of host chromosomes with divergent orthologs. We integrate microcell-mediated chromosome transfer with CRISPR/Cas9 to import the intact 152-Mb rat X chromosome into male mouse embryonic stem cells, and subsequently replace the mouse X chromosome, maintaining its stability and integrity. Rat-specific LINE1 and RatSatRep2 repeats recruit mouse SETDB1 inefficiently, causing local H3K9me3 loss. This triggers 3D remodeling, characterized by de novo topologically associating domain (TAD) boundaries that aberrantly activate adjacent genes, including Rhox5 , impairing differentiation. We provide a platform for dissecting sequence and epigenome cooperation in chromosome regulation, and evaluating fidelity of large-scale heterologous DNA.

raw_data.abstract: The mouse genome encodes two Lefty genes that antagonize NODAL signaling to break symmetry during gastrulation. Despite their central regulatory role, accurately describing and comparing their embryonic function remains unclear. Here, we generated high replicate powered single-cell transcriptional atlases of Lefty1 and Lefty2 mutant embryogenesis to evaluate the effects of perturbed NODAL signaling during gastrulation. We find that both mutants exhibit phenotypes beginning with the earliest primitive streak derivatives, suggesting a sequential shift from anterior Lefty1 to posterior Lefty2-based control that prevents spurious differentiation into extraembryonic and axial mesoendoderm at the cost of embryonic mesoderm and, in the case of Lefty1, rostral forebrain specification. By phasing bulk SMAD2/3 ChIP-seq data into single-cell-resolved descriptions of signal transduction, we identify distinct NODAL-responsive modules that track the context-specific use of this morphogen over gastrulation time. Collectively, our work highlights the potential of single-cell assays to decode how complex differentiation processes resolve morphogen signals in space and time.

raw_data.abstract: The rise of multidrug-resistant bacterial infections necessitates the discovery of novel antimicrobial strategies. Here, we show that protein design provides a generalizable means of generating new antimicrobials by neutralizing the function of bacterial adhesins, which are virulence factors critical in host-pathogen interactions. We de novo designed high-affinity miniprotein binders to FimH and Abp chaperone usher pili adhesins from uropathogenic Escherichia coli and Acinetobacter baumannii , respectively, which are implicated in mediating both uncomplicated and catheter-associated urinary tract infections (UTI) responsible for significant morbidity worldwide. The designed antagonists have high specificity and stability, disrupt bacterial recognition of host receptors, block biofilm formation, and are effective in treating and preventing murine models of uncomplicated and catheter-associated UTIs in vivo.

raw_data.abstract: In nature, nuclear DNA complexed with histone form highly condensed chromatin via loop extrusion and microphase separation, yielding physically constrained solid-like structures. Inspired by this natural compaction, here we demonstrate that freezing-induced crystallization pressure and freeze-concentration effects trigger solid-liquid microphase separation for efficient DNA compression. Freezing compress various nucleic acids (single stranded DNA, molecular beacons, siRNA, plasmid DNA) into high-density states that self-assemble into nanoparticles (DNA-NPs, MB-NPs, siBcl-2-NPs, siPLK1-NPs, pEGFP-NPs). Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that ice crystal growth increases solute concentration, enhancing DNA intermolecular interactions to form supramolecular chains. Stress at advancing ice-liquid interfaces further orders and compacts these supramolecular chains into nanoparticles. In breast cancer cells, MB-NPs detect miRNA-21; siBcl-2-NPs downregulate Bcl-2 protein; siPLK1-NPs exhibited antitumor effects; and pEGFP-NPs mediate green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression. This freeze-induced self-assembly strategy replaces chemical synthesis with physical constraints, establishing a versatile platform for facile production of nucleic acid nanoparticles.

raw_data.abstract: The enzymatic late-stage functionalization of C(sp 3 )-H bonds has emerged as a transformative strategy in medicinal chemistry. Verruculogen synthase (FtmOx1) is known to catalyze the endoperoxidation of its native substrate, fumitremorgin B. Here, we demonstrate the catalytic versatility of FtmOx1 by showing its ability to mediate diverse C(sp 3 )-H transformations on non-native substrates—phenethylamine and tetrahydroisoquinoline derivatives ( 1 ) —including β-hydroxylation, β-ketone formation, dealkylation, and α,β-desaturation. A total of 48 structurally diverse substrates prove suitable for this method, substantially expanding the biocatalytic repertoire of FtmOx1. Mechanistic studies, combined with crystallographic and mutagenesis analyses, reveal the distinct molecular basis for this diverse C(sp 3 )-H oxyfunctionalization compared to native pathway. Notably, the relative flexibility of the phenethyl and benzyl chains of 1 , assisted by specific substitutions that allow the two chains to swing, enables high β-selectivity for hydroxylation and prevents secondary oxidation. This C(sp 3 )-H activation platform efficiently generates structurally diverse oxyfunctionalized derivatives, including 1,2-amino alcohols ( 2 ), 1,2-amino ketones ( 3 ), and enamines ( 4 ), accelerating lead discovery for modulators of the human relaxin family peptide receptor 4 (RXFP4). Collectively, our work establishes FtmOx1 as a powerful biocatalytic tool, expanding the frontiers of C–H functionalization in drug discovery.
